claims.claim: Modernity has traditionally been presented as an age where artifacts supplant nature and destroy the natural environment through a process of de-naturalization, but Hannah Arendt questioned this view by arguing that a process of re-naturalization has taken place to the detriment of the human world.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Modernity, in philosophical and sociological literature, has “traditionally” been presented as the age when artifacts supplant nature and destroy the originally given natural environment. The process of modernization, from this point of view, is the process of de-naturalization . This widely shared conviction has ba - sically been questioned by Hannah Arendt. During the centuries of modern age, in the detriment of the commonly created and uphold human world, process of re-naturalization  has been taking place, Arendt argues.

claims.claim: Arendt subordinated the ecological connotations of the natural-artificial dichotomy in The Human Condition to the requirements of her political philosophy, worrying primarily about the threat of re-naturalization—embodying the victory of natural necessity over liberty—rather than the dominance of technology itself.
claims.supporting_excerpt: My hypothesis is, concerning the subject of this paper, that the ecological connotations of natural–artificial  dichotomy, in The Human Condition, were subordinated to the requirements of her political philosophy. She was worrying, first of all, not about the dominance of technology but the threat of re-naturalization (Villa 1996: 201) which, transposing it to the terms of political philosophy, for her, embodied the victory of natural necessity over liberty.

definitions.definition: The process of modernization viewed as the supplanting of nature by artifacts and the destruction of the originally given natural environment.
A process taking place during the modern age, enhanced by technology and resulting in world-alienation, to the detriment of the commonly created and upheld human world.

distinctions.distinction: The Arendtian critique of modernity, influenced by Martin Heidegger's philosophy, makes a difference between the notions of Earth and world.

must_not_be_lost: Arendt's transformation of the interpretation of the natural and artificial dichotomy inherited from German cultural criticism.
The integration of Heideggerian philosophy into a political philosophy based on the notion of plurality.
unresolved_context: Inter-war German cultural criticism and its dichotomies such as culture-civilization, life-spirit, community-society, and organic-mechanical.
The specific impact of American intellectual climate and everyday life impressions on Arendt's political thought.
